# kolonie-docs#412. These four lines drew the line between the Blocked column
# and the blocked-by relation in one place: the column waits on a person, the
# relation waits on work that is on the board, and so an issue blocked only by
# another issue could sit in Ready. The triage sweep now moves that issue into
# Blocked and back out again when its dependencies close, which makes the
# division false and the last sentence false outright. It is not a rewording —
# `agents/board.md` quotes the retired sentence and says what replaced it, so
# a reader who remembers the old rule is told it changed rather than left to
# notice. The distinction the first three lines drew is gone with it: the
# column now says *this is waiting*, whatever it is waiting for.
**This is not the Blocked column, and both stay.** The column is for waiting on a
person, a decision or a third party — something no issue on this board will
close. The relation is for waiting on work that is *on* the board. An issue whose
only blocker is another issue can sit in Ready: the queue already knows.

# kolonie-docs#493. The worker and the runners now read the same names —
# `LLM_GATEWAY_BASE_URL`, `LLM_GATEWAY_API_KEY_WORKER`, `LLM_GATEWAY_MODEL_WORKER`
# — so a line naming `OPENCODE_LLM_*` is a fact that stopped being one, not a
# line that moved. The replacement sits in architecture/automation.md, and the
# reason the names changed is measured there: on 2026-08-25 the triage pass
# answered 401 because a key rotated under one naming scheme left the other
# looking at a name nobody thought to look under.
| **The model** | **A setting, not a constant.** `OPENCODE_LLM_MODEL`, repository secret. Change the secret and the next scheduled run uses it; no model is named in `opencode.json` or in the workflow, and there is no committed default to fall back to |
| **Provider key and endpoint** | `OPENCODE_LLM_API_KEY` and `OPENCODE_LLM_BASE_URL`, repository secrets, both reaching opencode by `{env:…}` substitution in the committed `opencode.json`. **The URL is a secret and not merely the key**: it names a private endpoint, and a committed hostname is a target that stays reachable in git history after the line is deleted. `.github/scripts/no-gateway-leak.sh` greps the tree for both values on every run of `CI` and prints neither |

# kolonie-docs#494. The three lanes were named after the tool that ran them and
# one of those names had stopped being true: no maintainer used Claude Code any
# more, so `agent:claude` meant *a maintainer takes this* while `agent:opencode`
# meant *the unattended worker may*, and a maintainer labelling her package
# after the tool she was actually driving handed it to the worker. The lanes are
# now named after who decides — `queue:operator`, `queue:maintainer`,
# `queue:worker`, with the worker's markers as `worker:failed` and
# `worker:forbidden`.

# back into live documentation — the one thing #494 exists to remove.
#

# to retire prose: a line that lost content is still a lost line, and the check
# reports one that reappears.

# kolonie-platform#1684. These three lines said the Colony has no recovery of
# any kind. That stopped being true when opt-in, nominated-in-advance credential
# recovery shipped, so they are retired rather than moved: the sentence that
# replaces them in ARCHITECTURE.md keeps the property they were protecting — a
# lost key still cannot erase an account — and states why recovery does not
# weaken it. Restoring them would put a false claim back into live documentation.
- **No recovery.** A lost key means no erasure, matching what
  `onboarding/agent-guide.md` already tells an arriving agent about lost keys.
  Anything else would make the erasure path the account-takeover path.
